CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 115 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 6




              BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                          )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                            )
          FOR AN ORDER OF THE COMMISSION                               )
          APPROVING ITS NEW EXTRA LARGE LOAD                           )
          TARIFF AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF                           )   CAUSE NO. PUD 202600046
          SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                                 )
          CUSTOMERS AND A REGULATORY ASSET TO                          )
          RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                                )
          PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE                              )

                             REPLY BRIEF-IN-CHIEF OF WALMART INC.
                         REGARDING THE APPLICABILITY OF THE XLPL TARIFF

                Walmart Inc. ("Walmart") submits this Reply Brief pursuant to Order No. 7614491

         and in response to the Joint Brief in Chief of AARP, OIEC, OSN, Petroleum Alliance of

         Oklahoma and PUD Regarding Alternative Electric Service Frameworks (“Joint Parties

         Brief”), the Attorney General’s Brief-in-Chief (“AG Brief”) and the Brief in Chief of Google

         Regarding Alternative Electric Service Frameworks (“Google Brief”).

                Walmart does not advance an alternative electric service framework. Rather, it

         addresses Order No. 761449 item (g), which asks whether 17 O.S. § 903 requires

         separate tariffs for data center and other computational load customers in light of the 17

         O.S. § 901(4) definition of large load customers.2 More specifically, this Reply Brief

         addresses a related point not addressed by the opening briefs: the customers to whom

         the tariff may apply.


         I.     Summary

                Walmart generally supports the proposed provisions of OG&E's Extra Large

         Power and Light tariff ("XLPL") and its Terms and Conditions of Service for Extra Large


         1 Order Granting Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule in Order No. 758969 to Include a Briefing

         Schedule (Oct. 21, 2026).
         2 Id. at 4.
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 115 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 6


                                                  REPLY BRIEF-IN-CHIEF OF WALMART INC.
                                         REGARDING THE APPLICABILITY OF THE XLPL TARIFF
                                                               CAUSE NO. PUD 202600046

         Load Customers ("T&CXLLC"). Walmart’s concern is that the proposed definition of

         Large Load Customer is not consistent with the definition in House Bill 2992.3 The

         Commission should require OG&E to conform its definitions to the statute by expressly

         excluding residential, commercial, agricultural, and industrial ratepayers. Nothing in the

         Joint Parties Brief, the AG Brief or the Google Brief is to the contrary, because none of

         them address this exclusion.


         II.     The Statutory Class Is Defined, and Expressly Excludes Existing Ratepayer
                 Classes

                 The Joint Parties, the AG and Google agree that § 903 calls for one separate

         tariff for the class defined in § 901(4). The AG reads § 903 to require separate tariffs for

         data centers and other large computational loads meeting the § 901(4) threshold.4 The

         Joint Parties say the provisions require a separate tariff for large load customers as

         defined in § 901(4).5 They add that HB 2992 does not require a separate tariff for each

         end use within the definition.6 Google likewise argues that nothing in §§ 901(4) or 903

         prohibits a self-supply election within that tariff.7

                 However, those briefs quote only the first part of § 901(4): new data centers, new

         cryptocurrency mining operations, and new AI computing facilities contracting to add 75

         MW or more. None of the briefs mention the definition's last sentence, which states: "It

         does not include residential, commercial, agricultural, or industrial ratepayers."8 A plain

         4 AG Brief at 9.
         5 Joint Parties Brief at 21.

                                                              CAUSE NO. PUD 202600046

         reading of HB 2992 shows the Legislature intended the law to address specific

         customers.9

                  That exclusion is consistent with the Act's stated purpose. Section 902 directs the

         governing body to "ensure that residential, commercial, and industrial customers are

         protected from paying unjust rates resulting directly from electric service to large load

         customers."10 The AG cites the same provision.11 Commercial and industrial customers

         are among the customers the statute protects. They are not the customers it regulates.


         III.     The 75 MW Threshold Is Reasonable, but the Tariff's Definitions Leave a
                  Gap

                  Walmart supports the 75 MW threshold. That floor is consistent with the

         testimony of Walmart witness Michael Marchand about the intent of HB 2992.12 A lower

         threshold would create a significant risk of inadvertently capturing standard, stable

         commercial and industrial customers in the XLPL.13

                  The risk is real for retail operations. Modern omnichannel retailers increasingly

         use automated distribution or fulfillment operations, including refrigerated food

         distribution, that integrate electric trailer plugs and electric vehicle charging.14 The

         combined demand of such electrification-focused commercial facilities can approach or

         exceed 50 MW over a planning horizon.15 The 75 MW threshold provides a regulatory

         buffer that keeps standard retail and commercial distribution centers out of a tariff

                                                 REPLY BRIEF-IN-CHIEF OF WALMART INC.
                                        REGARDING THE APPLICABILITY OF THE XLPL TARIFF
                                                              CAUSE NO. PUD 202600046

         focused on more speculative loads, while still capturing system-impacting data centers

         and cryptocurrency operations.16

                   A numeric threshold is not a substitute for the statutory exclusion. Walmart's

         primary concern is that neither the XLPL's definition of Large Load Customer nor the

         T&CXLLC's definition of Customer expressly excludes residential, commercial,

         agricultural, or industrial ratepayers from the new tariff.17


         IV.       The Request Does Not Depend on the Act's Formal Application

                   Order No. 761449 notes that the Commission has recently held that a statute

         becoming effective after an application was filed did not apply or require particular

         treatment in that proceeding.18 Walmart's request does not turn on that question.

                   The Commission described OG&E's own application as filed "pursuant to House

         Bill 2992 and the Commission's Final Order No. 753440."19 OG&E invoked the Act in

         seeking this tariff and should not be heard to disclaim the Act's definition of the class it

         was written to serve. In any event, the cost-causation principle that supports the

         exclusion applies independently of the Act's effective date, because the Commission's

         core question is whether the tariff is lawful, just, reasonable, and in the public interest.20


         V.        Order No. 761612 and the Class-Wide Nature of the Inquiry

                   The Commission has held that the lawfulness of the XLPL tariff is a class-wide

                                                 REPLY BRIEF-IN-CHIEF OF WALMART INC.
                                        REGARDING THE APPLICABILITY OF THE XLPL TARIFF
                                                              CAUSE NO. PUD 202600046

         question: the tariff is either lawful or unlawful, and no individual consumer's load profile

         changes that calculus.21 Walmart's request is framed accordingly. It does not ask the

         Commission to evaluate any single customer's load. It asks that the tariff's definitions

         state who is and is not within the class.


         VI.       Relief Requested

                   Walmart respectfully requests that the Commission:

         1.        Require OG&E to amend the definition of Large Load Customer in the XLPL and
                   the definition of Customer in the T&CXLLC to conform to the statute by adding
                   language that specifically excludes residential, commercial, agricultural, and
                   industrial ratepayers, or entities that build generation for behind-the-meter
                   projects.

         2.        Hold that any separate tariff under § 903 applies to the class defined in § 901(4)
                   as a whole, and that existing ratepayer classes are not brought within it by
                   reason of size alone.

         3.        Provide that no approval of any alternative electric service framework alters the
                   foregoing, and reserve Walmart's right to respond to further briefing.
